newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish leaders say peace efforts at crucial point.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish leaders say peace efforts at crucial point.

text.p: Leaders of Northern Irish political parties linked to guerrilla groups said on Wednesday that efforts to secure peace in the province were at a critical point.

Gerry Adams, head of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, said in Belfast it was "a very, very crucial time" and urged British Prime Minister John Major to order his ministers to talk directly to his party.

In London, Gary McMichael of the Ulster Democratic Party said multi-party talks on the future of the province -- from which Sinn Fein is excluded because the IRA has not renewed its ceasefire -- "could conceivably collapse within days".

He said the talks process, seen as vital to persuading Protestant guerrilla groups to maintain their ceasefire, could collapse because of an impasse over when the talks should discuss the "decommissioning" or disposing of guerrilla weapons.
"Unless we can find the common ground and move forward and beyond the current debate on decommissioning then the process is in serious jeopardy," McMichael said after meeting Major.
Before going into the talks, Protestant leaders said they wanted reassurances from Britain that it was not doing secret deals with the IRA.
Adams said Britain, which has refused Sinn Fein direct contact since the IRA ditched a 17-month ceasefire in February, had failed to respond to moves which could lead to a new truce.

He said he and moderate nationalist leader John Hume were working to restore the peace process and Sinn Fein had had direct contacts with United States and Irish officials. "We have no direct contact with the British government."

"So far Sinn Fein are still waiting for the British government to respond to different suggestions which have been made to get a complete restoration of the peace process," he said, without being more specific.
Earlier Major said the province's political process had run into "a sticky patch", but he hoped problems would be overcome.
"At this very very crucial time...the onus is on the British government to meet Sinn Fein to try to resolve these difficulties", Adams told reporters.
Britain and Ireland say a decision to admit Sinn Fein to talks hinges on a declaration of a credible IRA truce.
Senior Sinn Fein strategist Martin McGuinness last week laid out a list of demands that he hinted could lead to a IRA truce.
These included a guaranteed place for Sinn Fein in talks with a defined time-table and a British pledge that the IRA would not have to surrender guns as the price of progress.
London says the IRA will have to prove by "more than soft words" the dependibility of any future cessation.
Irish and British government ministers were meeting in Belfast later on Wednesday to discuss the peace process.
